# NYU SPS MS in Management and Analytics — Research Handbook

Oct 17, 2026 · @Shradha

## How to read this handbook

This handbook covers the NYU SPS MS in Management and Analytics as publicly documented on the research date above, for a January 2027 entrant starting with limited programming, SQL and maths background. Every claim carries one of four labels so you can tell evidence from interpretation.

| Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Official** | Stated on an NYU-owned page (SPS programme page, bulletin, faculty page, NYU news) |
| **Source-supported** | Stated on a credible non-NYU page (published bio, LinkedIn public preview, news) |
| **Inference** | My reasoning from official facts, such as likely tools or difficulty |
| **Not publicly verified** | Could not be confirmed from public sources; ask NYU |

Limits worth knowing up front: I cannot log in to LinkedIn, Albert (NYU's registration system) or NYU Brightspace, so section-level instructor assignments and full syllabi are only as good as what NYU publishes openly. Where those gaps matter, the final section lists exactly what to ask the department.

## 1. Programme overview (Deliverable 1A)

The MS in Management and Analytics (MSMA) is a 36-credit, 12-course, STEM-designated degree: 8 core courses, a 2-course concentration, 1 elective and a capstone. **Official**, per the [2026–2027 NYU Bulletin](https://bulletins.nyu.edu/graduate/professional-studies/programs/management-analytics-ms/) and the [SPS programme page](https://www.sps.nyu.edu/explore/degrees-and-programs/ms-in-management-and-analytics.html). It is run by the Management & Technology department in the Division of Programs in Business, and it replaced the older MS in Management and Systems (students admitted under that name follow the 2023–24 bulletin).

### Key facts

| Item | Detail | Label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Credits | 36 (12 courses × 3 credits) | Official |
| Duration | Minimum 18 months full-time (3 terms × 12 credits in the sample plan); bulletin text says "two years full-time or up to five years part-time" | Official |
| Starts | Fall or Spring | Official |
| STEM | Yes, CIP 11.1099 (eligible for 24-month STEM OPT extension) | Official |
| Format | Bulletin: on-site, Manhattan campus, day and evening classes. Programme page: onsite or hybrid, and says it "may be completed 100% online" | Official, but conflicting |
| Tuition | $2,896 per credit; $28,664 per term at 10–12 credits (Fall 2026 / Spring 2027), roughly $104,000 tuition for 36 credits before fees | Official (total is my arithmetic) |
| Spring 2027 deadlines | Regular Oct 1, 2026; Final Nov 15, 2026 (decision Dec 20, 2026) | Official |
| Admission | US bachelor's or international equivalent; holistic review | Official |
| Graduation | Complete 36 credits as listed; internship course needs 18+ credits and 3.0 GPA to apply | Official. Minimum overall GPA to graduate: Not publicly verified here (check SPS academic policies) |

The tuition figure matters for your planning: your existing school-comparison notes estimate about $60,000 for NYU SPS, which is well below the official per-credit rate.

The elective can also be another concentration's foundation course, a course from another Division of Programs in Business master's, or the Real World course (RWLD1-GC 3050). **Official.** The MASY1-GC inventory also lists older courses (for example Strategic Marketing, Financial Management, Data Mining and Data Warehousing) that belong to the legacy Management and Systems degree; whether MSMA students can take them as the elective is **Not publicly verified**.

### Inconsistencies to raise with NYU

- **Concentration names.** The bulletin lists Business Analytics, Risk Analytics, Business Informatics and Applied Research. The programme page names Business Informatics, Risk Analytics and Business Analysis. The 2025–26 bulletin text used Data Analytics and Business Analysis instead.
- **Format.** Bulletin says on-site only; the programme page offers online and hybrid. For F-1 status this matters, so get the in-person requirement in writing.
- **Certifications FAQ.** The programme page attributes CISA to ISC2; CISA is actually issued by ISACA (CISSP is ISC2). Treat that FAQ as marketing copy rather than a curriculum statement.

### How the pieces fit together

The structure runs from tools to judgement. Quantitative Methods and Database Management give you statistics and SQL in term 1. Data-Driven Decision-Making and your concentration foundation apply them in term 2. Advanced analytics, Emerging Technologies and the Applied Technical Project capstone convert them into recommendations in term 3. The management courses (team skills, change, project management, risk) run in parallel so that, by the capstone, you can scope, staff and defend a data project rather than only analyse one. **Inference** from the official sample plan and prerequisite chain.

For your goal of marketing analytics, the **Business Analytics** concentration is the natural fit: it is the only one with hands-on visualisation, predictive modelling and machine learning. MSMA has no dedicated marketing course in its required list, so marketing context would have to come through your capstone topic, the elective slot, or a course borrowed from the MS in Integrated Marketing. **Inference**; confirm cross-registration rules with your adviser.

## 2. Subject-by-subject breakdown (Deliverable 1B)

NYU publishes official course descriptions and prerequisites, but no week-by-week modules, assessment weights or reading lists for MSMA courses are publicly available; syllabi sit behind NYU Brightspace. So in each entry below, **Official** covers the bulletin title, code, credits, description and prerequisites from the [MASY1-GC course inventory](https://bulletins.nyu.edu/graduate/professional-studies/courses/masy1-gc/). Everything under "Likely tools", "Likely assessment", "Suggested reading" and "Difficulty" is **Inference**: what a course with that description typically involves, not an NYU statement. Module names, exam formats and reading lists are **Not publicly verified** for every course.

### MASY1-GC 1015 · Quantitative Methods for Business Analysis · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** a foundational statistics course covering descriptive univariate statistics, bivariate association, introductory multivariate analysis, estimation and inference, tests of difference, significance and hypothesis testing, all taught with real industry data. No listed prerequisite, but it is a prerequisite for 1215, 1800, 2000, 2400 and 2600, making it the gateway course of the degree.

- **Core topics (from description):** mean, median, variance, distributions; correlation and cross-tabs; confidence intervals; t-tests, chi-square, ANOVA-type tests of difference; p-values and hypothesis testing; an introduction to multiple regression.
- **Likely tools (Inference):** Excel with the Analysis ToolPak, and possibly SPSS, JMP or R. The department's elective 3100 uses SPSS and SAS/JMP, which hints at the house toolset.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** weekly problem sets, a data-analysis project on a real dataset, and a midterm and/or final.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** sampling distributions, interpreting p-values correctly, and choosing the right test for the data type.
- **Suggested reading (my suggestion, not NYU's):** *OpenIntro Statistics* (free PDF); *Naked Statistics* by Charles Wheelan for intuition.
- **Career relevance:** every A/B test, campaign lift analysis and survey you will run in marketing analytics rests on this course.

### MASY1-GC 1500 · Database Management · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** an introductory course on data extraction, manipulation, analysis and management with relational database systems, taught through lectures, hands-on computer exercises, widely used databases and real-world database projects. Prerequisite for 1215, 2000 and 2200.

- **Core topics:** relational model, tables, keys and relationships; data organisation structures; SQL for querying and manipulation.
- **Likely tools (Inference):** SQL on MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server or Oracle; ER-diagramming tools.
- **Likely concepts (Inference):** SELECT/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING, JOINs, subqueries, normalisation (1NF–3NF), ER modelling, indexes.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** SQL lab exercises and a database design project.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** JOIN logic, GROUP BY with aggregation, and normalisation.
- **Suggested reading:** *Learning SQL* by Alan Beaulieu; SQLBolt and Mode's SQL tutorial (free).
- **Career relevance:** SQL is the single most requested skill in analyst job postings; you will use it daily for customer, campaign and sales data.

### MASY1-GC 1600 · Managing Technical Projects · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** fundamentals of project management for technology projects: defining a business problem, planning a solution and managing quality delivery. Prerequisite for 1315, 2400 and 2600.

- **Likely frameworks (Inference):** PMBOK process groups, scope/WBS, Gantt charts and critical path, risk registers, stakeholder analysis, Agile/Scrum versus waterfall.
- **Likely tools (Inference):** MS Project, Smartsheet, Jira, Trello or Asana.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** a team project plan for a technology initiative, plus case discussions.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** critical-path scheduling and earned-value calculations, if covered.
- **Career relevance:** analytics projects fail more often from scoping than from maths; this course also maps toward CAPM/PMP certification.

### MASY1-GC 1700 · Organizational Risk Management and Information Security · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** protecting data and information as it relates to strategy, policy, awareness, data classification, ownership, accountability, monitoring and reporting; network security components; preventive and detective tools (anti-malware, access control lists, cryptography, intrusion detection, audit logs, logical and physical controls); and information risk assessment.

- **Likely frameworks (Inference):** CIA triad, NIST Cybersecurity Framework, ISO 27001, risk matrices (likelihood × impact).
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** an information risk assessment of a case organisation, quizzes on terminology.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** networking vocabulary (firewalls, protocols, encryption types).
- **Career relevance:** customer data privacy (GDPR, CCPA) is now central to marketing analytics, especially with first-party data.

### MASY1-GC 1115 · Management Skills for Technology Professionals · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** working effectively with others, in teams and as a leader; self-awareness, mobilising others, problem-solving and reaching agreement, through analysis of real business issues and skill-building activities.

- **Likely frameworks (Inference):** team development models (Tuckman), emotional intelligence, negotiation (BATNA), conflict styles, feedback models.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** reflections, self-assessments, team exercises, case analyses.
- **Career relevance:** analysts who can present and persuade get promoted; this complements your existing brand-management experience.

### MASY1-GC 1215 · Data-Driven Decision-Making · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** analysing operational and strategic situations and selecting optimal courses of action using quantitative tools. **Prerequisites:** 1015 and 1500. Prerequisite for the capstone.

- **Likely topics (Inference):** decision trees and expected value, linear programming and optimisation (Excel Solver), sensitivity and what-if analysis, forecasting, simulation (Monte Carlo), KPI design.
- **Likely tools (Inference):** Excel Solver and Data Tables; possibly Python or R.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** modelling assignments and a decision-analysis case project.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** formulating an optimisation problem (objective, constraints) from a business story.
- **Suggested reading:** *Business Analytics: Data Analysis and Decision Making* by Albright and Winston is a common text for courses of this type.
- **Career relevance:** budget allocation across channels, pricing and media-mix decisions are optimisation problems.

### MASY1-GC 1315 · Managing Change and Innovation · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** structural, process, technological and human change dynamics; organisational development and change models; readiness and assessment tools; metrics to benchmark progress; diffusion of innovation and creative destruction; company case studies. **Prerequisite:** 1600.

- **Likely frameworks (Inference):** Lewin's unfreeze–change–refreeze, Kotter's 8 steps, ADKAR, Rogers' diffusion of innovations, Schumpeter's creative destruction.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** case write-ups, a change-readiness audit, presentations.
- **Career relevance:** getting a business to act on an analytics insight is a change-management problem.

### MASY1-GC 1800 · Emerging Technologies · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** impacts of new and rapidly evolving technologies on organisations; disruption; designing projects that implement new technologies; adoption challenges; legal and privacy issues; and a course-long case study project identifying and implementing a technology for an organisation. **Prerequisites:** 1015 and 1315.

- **Likely topics (Inference):** generative and agentic AI (the programme page highlights applied and agentic AI and AI safety), cloud, blockchain, IoT, automation; technology adoption models.
- **Assessment:** the course-long case study project is **Official**; other components are Not publicly verified.
- **Career relevance:** AI in marketing (personalisation, content generation, attribution) is a strong capstone and interview theme.

### MASY1-GC 2000 · Foundations of Business Analytics · 3 credits (Business Analytics concentration)

**Official description, summarised:** turning business data into actionable information; using analytical and data-visualisation software to clean, manage and prepare data; exploration, summarisation, visualisation, interactive exploratory analytics and introductory predictive analytics on real-world datasets, leading to strategic recommendations. Hands-on, instructor-guided. **Prerequisites:** 1015 and 1500.

- **Likely tools (Inference):** Tableau or Power BI for dashboards; Excel; possibly Python (pandas) or R for cleaning.
- **Likely concepts (Inference):** data cleaning and missing values, EDA, chart selection and dashboard design, data storytelling, simple linear and logistic regression.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** dashboard assignments and a final analytics project with a recommendation presentation.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** data preparation (joins, reshaping, messy data) usually takes longer than the visualisation itself.
- **Suggested reading:** *Storytelling with Data* by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic.
- **Career relevance:** this is the core day-to-day skill set of a marketing or business analyst role.

### MASY1-GC 2100 · Advanced Business Analytics · 3 credits (Business Analytics concentration)

**Official description, summarised:** an applied machine-learning course: the end-to-end predictive process, feature extraction and selection, essential algorithms, model evaluation, and case studies in supervised and unsupervised learning including prediction, classification and text analytics. **Prerequisite:** 2000.

- **Likely tools (Inference):** Python with scikit-learn, pandas and Jupyter; possibly R.
- **Likely algorithms (Inference):** linear and logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, k-NN, k-means clustering, basic NLP (bag-of-words, sentiment).
- **Likely concepts (Inference):** train/test split, cross-validation, overfitting, confusion matrix, precision/recall, ROC-AUC, feature engineering.
- **Likely assessment (Inference):** coding notebooks and a predictive modelling project.
- **Hardest for a beginner:** coding fluency in Python, and understanding why a model generalises or overfits.
- **Suggested reading:** *An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python* (free PDF); *Data Science for Business* by Provost and Fawcett.
- **Career relevance:** churn prediction, customer segmentation, propensity modelling and review sentiment are the most common marketing ML use cases.

### MASY1-GC 4115 · Applied Technical Project (capstone) · 3 credits

**Official description, summarised:** under a faculty supervisor, students select a topic or undertake a real-world project for active practitioners, then produce a practical application demonstrating professional-level mastery, reviewed by the supervisor and one other expert. **Prerequisites:** 1215 and 1315.

- **Assessment:** supervisor plus a second expert review is **Official**; deliverable format (report, presentation, prototype) is Not publicly verified.
- **Advice (Inference):** pick a marketing-analytics problem (for example a customer segmentation or campaign attribution study) so the capstone becomes your portfolio centrepiece.

### Elective options

**MASY1-GC 3030 · Syntax Language Programming.** **Official:** for students with some Python and/or R; reviews fundamentals, then classes, object-oriented design, decorators and generators; Pandas, NumPy and R Shiny; Git and code review; benchmarking, profiling and testing; ends with interview preparation. Beginner difficulty: high. Best elective for a technical analytics career, but only if you arrive with Python basics.

**MASY1-GC 3100 · Application-Based Programming.** **Official:** point-and-click analysis in SPSS or SAS/JMP; data wrangling and restructuring, then descriptive, associative and predictive analysis (regression, decision trees) and creating reusable syntax. Beginner difficulty: medium. SPSS skills are valued in market research and consumer insights firms.

**MASY1-GC 3260 · Advanced Data Warehousing Applications.** **Official:** data warehouse concepts, sourcing strategy, ETL, the CRISP data-mining approach, data security and ethics. Useful for BI and data engineering paths.

**MASY1-GC 3415 · Special Topics in Management and Analytics.** **Official:** a seminar whose title and content change each offering. Check the term's class search for the current topic.

**MASY1-GC 3910 · Internship.** **Official:** supervised on-site work for academic credit; requires 18 credits and a 3.0 GPA. For F-1 students this is typically how Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is authorised (Inference; confirm with NYU Office of Global Services).

## 3. Beginner preparation roadmap (Deliverable 1C)

If you start in Spring 2027 (late January), you have about 14 weeks. Spend most of them on three things in this order: statistics, SQL, then Python. Those feed the two term-1 technical courses (1015, 1500) and everything in the Business Analytics concentration. This whole section is **my recommendation**; the resources are free and widely used, not NYU-assigned.

### Priority order

1. **Statistics (for 1015, 1215, 2000, 2100).** Highest priority, because 1015 gates five later courses.
2. **SQL (for 1500, 1215, 2000).** Second, because it is learnable fast and pays off immediately.
3. **Excel modelling (for 1015, 1215).** Pivot tables, lookups, Solver, Data Analysis ToolPak.
4. **Python with pandas (for 2100, 3030, possibly 2000).** Needed by term 3 at the latest, but it takes the longest to become fluent.
5. **Visualisation with Tableau or Power BI (for 2000, capstone).** Quick to learn once you have data skills.
6. **Project management and security vocabulary (for 1600, 1700).** Light reading only.

### 14-week plan (about 8–10 hours a week)

| Weeks | Focus | What to do | Resources (free) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–4 | Statistics foundations | Descriptive stats, probability, distributions, sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, correlation, simple regression. Do the exercises, not only videos | Khan Academy "Statistics and Probability"; StatQuest (YouTube, Josh Starmer); *OpenIntro Statistics* (free PDF, openintro.org) |
| 3–7 | SQL | SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY/HAVING, JOINs, subqueries, CASE, then window functions. Aim to solve 50+ practice problems | SQLBolt; Mode SQL Tutorial; Kaggle Learn "Intro to SQL" and "Advanced SQL"; HackerRank or LeetCode SQL (easy tier) |
| 5–8 | Excel for analysis | Pivot tables, XLOOKUP, conditional logic, charts, Data Analysis ToolPak (t-tests, regression), Solver for a simple optimisation | Microsoft Learn Excel training; ExcelJet; Chandoo.org |
| 7–12 | Python and pandas | Variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions; then pandas (read, filter, group, merge), matplotlib/seaborn. Use Jupyter or Google Colab | Kaggle Learn "Python", "Pandas", "Data Visualization"; *Python for Everybody* (Charles Severance, free); freeCodeCamp "Data Analysis with Python" |
| 10–13 | Dashboards | Rebuild one marketing dataset as an interactive dashboard; publish it | Tableau Public free training videos, or Microsoft Learn Power BI "Data Analyst" path |
| 13–14 | Light reading for management courses | Project management basics (scope, WBS, Agile), CIA triad and NIST CSF basics | Google Project Management certificate (audit on Coursera); NIST CSF 2.0 overview on nist.gov |

### Per-course preparation

| Course | Learn before term | Most important concept | Connects to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1015 Quantitative Methods | Distributions, sampling, hypothesis testing, regression basics | Choosing and interpreting the right test | 1215, 1800, 2000, 2400, 2600 |
| 1500 Database Management | SQL querying, JOINs, ER diagrams | JOINs and aggregation | 1215, 2000, 2200, 3260 |
| 1600 Managing Technical Projects | Scope, WBS, Gantt, Agile vocabulary | Defining scope from a business problem | 1315, 2400, 2600, capstone |
| 1700 Risk and Info Security | CIA triad, threat/vulnerability/risk, basic network terms | Risk = likelihood × impact | 2200, 2300 |
| 1115 Management Skills | None needed | Team dynamics | All group projects |
| 1215 Data-Driven Decision-Making | Excel Solver, expected value, decision trees | Formulating objective and constraints | Capstone |
| 1315 Managing Change | Kotter, Lewin (one article each) | Adoption barriers | 1800, capstone |
| 2000 Foundations of BA | Pandas or Excel cleaning, one dashboard | Data preparation | 2100, capstone |
| 1800 Emerging Technologies | Follow AI-in-business news | Adoption business case | Capstone |
| 2100 Advanced BA | Python + pandas; regression; train/test split | Overfitting and evaluation metrics | Capstone; job interviews |
| 3030 Syntax Language Programming | Python fundamentals through functions | Writing clean, reusable code | 2100 |
| 4115 Capstone | Collect 2–3 marketing problem ideas and public datasets | Scoping a feasible question | Synthesises the degree |

### Practice that compounds

Pick one marketing dataset early (Kaggle has e-commerce, customer-churn and marketing-campaign datasets) and run it through every skill as you learn it: summarise it with statistics, store and query it in SQL, clean it in pandas, dashboard it in Tableau, and finally build a churn or segmentation model. By January you would have a portfolio piece that previews 1015, 1500, 2000 and 2100, and a candidate capstone topic.

## 4. Professor research directory (Deliverable 2)

That listing is the strongest public evidence available, so in this directory **"Listed"** means the course appears under "Courses" on the instructor's official sps.nyu.edu profile. It does not tell you which term or section they will teach; section-level assignments for Spring 2027 are only visible in NYU's Albert class search once published. **Not publicly verified** applies to every term-specific assignment.

Two timing points to check with the department: whether term 2 can be Summer 2027 (1215 is officially "typically offered Fall and Spring", so a Fall 2027 term 2 is safer), and whether a January start follows the same order as the sample plan.

**How to confirm your actual instructors.** Term-specific assignments are published only in NYU's [public class search](https://bulletins.nyu.edu/class-search/), which I can't query from here, and later in Albert once you are admitted. In the class search, select the Spring 2027 term, type MASY1-GC in the search box, and open each section of 1015, 1500, 1600 and 1700: each one shows its instructor, meeting time and instruction mode. Many sections show no named instructor until a few weeks before term, so check again in December and early January.

### Individual profiles (most relevant to you)

**Andrew D. Banasiewicz — Clinical Professor; Academic Director, MSMA.** **Official:** BS Northwestern State University, MBA Louisiana Tech, PhD in business from Louisiana State University; nearly 20 years in corporate analytics roles and about 15 as a full-time professor; founder of Erudite Analytics, a consultancy estimating executive risk exposure; author of eight books including *Probabilistic Benchmarking* (2024), *Data Analytic Literacy* (2023), *Organizational Learning in the Age of Data* (2021) and *Evidence-Based Decision-Making* (2019). Listed for 1015, 2000, 2200 and the capstone. **Why he matters to you:** as academic director he shapes the curriculum and advises students, and he may teach your two most foundational analytics courses. Reading *Data Analytic Literacy* before you start would be a direct preview of how the programme frames analytics (Inference).

**Kenechukwu ("Ken") Ezekwem — Clinical Assistant Professor.** **Official:** PhD, MS, MBA and two graduate certificates from North Dakota State University; work at the intersection of analytics, AI and operations; teaches database management, quantitative methods and experimental design with a "hands-on, governance-minded" approach using contemporary programming languages and enterprise platforms; research on turning messy unstructured data into usable data and integrating AI reasoning into business processes. Listed for 1015, 1500 and 3260. **Source-supported** (his public LinkedIn): graduate certificates in Business Analytics (2020) and Statistics (2019), and an accredited Scrum Master certification (2015). **Why he matters:** likely to teach one or both of your term-1 technical courses; his emphasis on programming suggests you should arrive with SQL and some Python (Inference).

**Andres Fortino — Clinical Associate Professor.** **Official:** PhD engineer who did device research at IBM Research; three patents; IEEE Senior Member; twelve books and over 80 publications; teaches graduate courses in AI, business analytics, data mining and research methods; among the first at SPS to integrate generative AI into coursework, using tools like ChatGPT in project work; described as designing project-based capstones that often lead to publications. **Assignment caveat:** his current profile confirms 1215, 1800, 2400, 2500, 3415 and the 4115 capstone (see the follow-up table above). **Why he matters:** strongest public evidence of how AI is used inside the programme, and a natural capstone mentor for an AI-in-marketing project.

**Regina Chang — Clinical Assistant Professor.** **Official:** listed for 1215 Data-Driven Decision-Making and 2100 Advanced Business Analytics. No biography, degrees or LinkedIn are published. **Why she matters:** as a full-time faculty member on both of your heaviest quantitative courses, she is worth looking up again closer to registration.

**Eleftheria K. Pissadaki — Instructor (designation not shown in result).** **Official:** interdisciplinary systems researcher spanning neuroscience, biology and mathematics; industry and academic experience with IBM, Biogen, the UK Medical Research Council and the University of Oxford; mentors applied projects (smart-city databases, AI in database systems, fraud detection); students have won capstone awards and published at conferences. Listed for 2000, 2100, 3505, and also for INTG1-GC1055 Statistical Measurements and MKAN1-UC5103 **Marketing Analytics**. **Why she matters:** the only MSMA instructor found who also teaches marketing analytics, which makes her the closest faculty match to your career goal (Inference).

**Rajeev Maharaj — Adjunct Instructor.** **Official:** Generative AI Scientist; previously Decision Sciences Specialist at Volkswagen Credit building ML and AI systems for a $30 billion auto-finance portfolio; dual master's from NYU Stern (Risk Management; Business Analytics), MBA Hofstra, BA Economics Queens College. Listed for 1015 and 2100; his bio confirms he teaches Advanced Business Analytics. **Why he matters:** a current industry practitioner for the ML course.

**Steven W. Goss — Clinical Professor; Chair, Management and Technology.** **Official:** BS Penn State, MA NYU, EdD in Instructional Technology and Media from Teachers College, Columbia; awards from AACE and the Online Learning Consortium for research on learner-centred online education. Listed for 1315 and the capstone.

**Other listed instructors, briefly.** Ronnie Obadiah (BA Maths and CS Cornell, NYU Stern MBA; leads master and reference data transformation in Citi's Chief Data Office; 1315, 1500). Amit S. Patel (Oracle Certified Professional, PMP; also teaches at NYU Tandon; 1500, 3100, 3260). Joseph Ng (former head of a global AI community of practice at a large financial firm; NYU MS in Management and Systems alumnus; 1800, capstone). Samuel Sultan (25+ years in software engineering and ERP; cites top student evaluations; 3030). Bohdan Hawryluk (NYU MS Management and Systems; Goldman Sachs, Weill Cornell, City of New York; 3030). Peter Peng (NYU MS Management and Systems; UBS and Citigroup IT; 1115). Lawrence Marciano Jr. (NYU MBA, BS Vanderbilt; Director at RBC Capital Markets; 1115, Internship). The 1600 project-management instructors bring mostly Agile and Scrum practitioner backgrounds.

## 5. Alumni research directory (Deliverable 3)

I could not verify a single graduate who holds the degree under its current name, MS in Management and Analytics. Every publicly documented alumnus graduated from its predecessor, the **MS in Management and Systems (MASY)**. NYU itself treats them as the same programme: the MSMA programme page features Bhavana Singh '17 as an "MS in Management and Analytics" alumna even though her own story says she earned the MS in Management and Systems, and NYU tags MASY alumni news with the MSMA programme label. So these alumni are the right evidence base, with one caveat: the MASY curriculum differed (it had concentrations such as Database Technologies, Strategy and Leadership, Enterprise Risk Management), so their outcomes are a guide, not a prediction.

The sample is small (8 alumni with any public career detail) and selected by NYU for promotion, so it is **not representative** of a graduating class. LinkedIn profiles are "Not publicly verified" unless stated, because I cannot log in to LinkedIn and none of these alumni's profiles surfaced in public search results.

### Alumni stories worth reading in full

**Sumit Gupta '15 (CVS Health).** NYU reports that he built a live, machine-learning COVID resource prediction tool used by more than 110 million people within three months during the pandemic, and leads work on health equity and bias in AI. He credits hands-on group work with industry-experienced instructors, and advises students to stay close to classmates. **Learning example:** the clearest public case of this degree leading to a data science role.

**Samarth Bedakihale '16 (PwC).** Came from a computer science and Nokia R&D background and used the degree to move from engineering into a techno-functional consulting role; he describes culture shock and communication barriers early on, and making heavy use of events and networking. **Learning example:** for a career switcher, the degree's management side mattered as much as its technical side.

**Bhavana Singh '17 (cybersecurity).** A Mumbai-raised former international student. Her capstone with NYU's Global Office of Information Security was a risk assessment of mobile-device use at NYU with mitigation strategies, which she says became a resume highlight. She won the NYU President's Service Award and an OGS International Student Leadership award, and recommends that incoming students learn relational and big-data databases, SQL, Python, JIRA, Tableau, Power BI and the basics of machine learning and generative AI. Her strongest advice: go beyond the classroom, join clubs and attend events across SPS and other NYU schools. **Learning example:** a capstone done with a real internal client can carry your first job search.

## 6. Integrated insights and recommendations (Deliverable 4)

The bottom line: MSMA is a management-and-technology degree with one genuinely analytical track, so its value for a marketing-analytics career depends on choosing the Business Analytics concentration, arriving with SQL, statistics and basic Python, and bending the capstone and elective toward marketing. Each answer below is labelled as an **Observed pattern** (from the sources) or an **Assumption / recommendation** (my judgement).

### Your questions, answered

**1. Most important subjects for a strong foundation.** 1015 Quantitative Methods and 1500 Database Management. *Observed:* together they are prerequisites for 1215, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2400 and 2600. Then 2000 and 2100 for analytics depth, and 1215 for decision modelling.

**2. Subjects needing the most advance preparation.** *Assumption:* 2100 Advanced Business Analytics (machine learning, coding), 1015 (statistics), 3030 Syntax Language Programming (its official description assumes some Python or R), and 1500 (SQL). *Observed:* Ezekwem's official bio says his database and quantitative courses use contemporary programming languages.

**3. Professors most relevant to your goals.** *Assumption, based on official bios:* Eleftheria Pissadaki, the only MSMA instructor found who also teaches Marketing Analytics; Andrew Banasiewicz, academic director and author on data-driven decision-making; Regina Chang and Rajeev Maharaj for 1215 and 2100; Andres Fortino as a possible capstone mentor on AI.

**4. Skills and tools that recur.** *Observed* across course descriptions, faculty bios and alumni advice: SQL and relational databases; statistics; Python (pandas, NumPy); data visualisation (Tableau, Power BI named by an alumna); machine learning; generative AI; project management and Agile/Scrum; data governance and risk. SPSS and SAS/JMP appear in one elective.

**5. Industries and functions among verified alumni.** *Observed (n = 6 with any role detail):* financial services and fintech IT (3), consulting (1), healthcare analytics (1), cybersecurity (1). Functions: data science, data strategy consulting, IT and programme management, security leadership. NYU's own Lightcast-sourced list adds Accenture, Amazon, Apple, Bloomberg, Deloitte, EY, Goldman Sachs, KPMG, Microsoft, Nielsen and PwC, which is broader but not individually verifiable.

**6. Career paths supported by the evidence.** Data science and analytics (Gupta), analytics and data-strategy consulting (Bedakihale), technology risk and security (Singh), and financial-services technology management (Peng, Ng, Hawryluk). **Marketing analytics is not represented** in any verified alumni story I found. *Observed;* this is the single most important gap for you.

**7. What distinguishes alumni in strong roles.** *Observed:* prior technical work experience before NYU (Gupta's path not stated; Bedakihale and Singh both had engineering or developer backgrounds); a capstone with a real client (Singh); heavy use of events, clubs and networking (Bedakihale, Singh). *Assumption:* coming from marketing rather than engineering, your differentiator will be domain knowledge plus demonstrable technical skill, so a portfolio matters more for you than for them.

**8. Knowledge gaps to close before starting.** In priority order: statistics, SQL, Excel modelling, Python with pandas, one BI tool. See section 3.

**9. Trajectories to learn from.** Singh's capstone model (real internal client, risk assessment with recommendations) is the most directly copyable; Gupta's shows how far the analytics track can go. *Recommendation:* design your capstone around a marketing client problem, such as segmentation, churn or attribution for an NYC brand or an NYU unit.

**10. What to ask NYU.** See the list below.

### Fit for you specifically

| Dimension | Score /10 | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Curriculum fit (marketing analytics transition) | 6 | Strong analytics core but no marketing course in the required list |
| Career outcome alignment | 5 | No verified marketing-analytics alumni; outcomes skew to finance, consulting, tech |
| Technical depth (SQL, Python, modelling) | 8 | SQL, statistics, ML and programming electives all present |
| OPT / visa pathway | 9 | STEM-designated (CIP 11.1099) |
| Cost vs value | 5 | About $104,000 tuition at the published per-credit rate |

These scores are **my assessment**, more cautious than the 8/10 in your earlier school-comparison notes, mainly because of the cost correction and the lack of marketing-specific evidence. Your MMS in Marketing actually complements the gap: you bring the domain, MSMA supplies the technical layer.
